title: A Christmas Carol
author: Charles Dickens
setting: The City of London and Camden Town, across a single Christmas Eve and Christmas Day
lengthNote: Five staves, around 30,000 words — short enough to be read aloud in an evening, which is what Dickens did with it
openingLine: Marley was dead, to begin with.
summary: A moneylender who has organised his whole life around refusal is visited in one night by his dead partner and three spirits, and shown his own childhood, the households he has never entered and a grave nobody visits. Dickens calls the divisions staves rather than chapters because the book is meant to be performed, and the argument is not that Scrooge feels sorry but that he pays, visits and turns up the next morning.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of A Christmas Carol
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription of Dickens's text. References give the stave, which is the only division the book itself uses.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Chapman and Hall, as A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas.

atAGlance.label: Illustrator
atAGlance.note: Four hand-coloured plates and four wood engravings for the first edition.

atAGlance.label: Divisions
atAGlance.note: A stave is the ruled set of lines music is written on; the title promises a carol, and the book keeps the promise.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: Everything between Marley's arrival and the Christmas morning bells happens in a few hours of story time.

structure.label: Stave I
structure.title: Marley's Ghost
structure.summary: Scrooge is defined entirely by what he turns away: his nephew's invitation, two charity collectors, his clerk's fire. Then his dead partner arrives dragging the cash-boxes and ledgers he accumulated instead of a life, and promises three more visitors.

scenes.summary: Fred offers dinner and is refused; the charity collectors are told about prisons and the surplus population.
Marley's face appears in the door knocker, and Scrooge explains it away by arguing with his own digestion.
The ghost states the book's thesis — that mankind, not the ledger, was his business — and names the terms of the visitations.

structure.label: Stave II
structure.title: The First of the Three Spirits
structure.summary: The Ghost of Christmas Past shows scenes Scrooge cannot alter and does not dispute: the boy left at school, Fezziwig's ball, and Belle releasing him from an engagement he has already broken in everything but name. The spirit never argues; it simply declines to stop.

scenes.summary: A solitary child left behind at the holidays, and an old man crying at the sight of himself.
An employer who spends a small sum and buys enormous happiness, which Scrooge himself points out.
She names the golden idol that has displaced her, and asks whether he would choose her now.

structure.label: Stave III
structure.title: The Second of the Three Spirits
structure.summary: The present is shown as a series of doors opening: the Cratchits' dinner in Camden Town, Fred's party, miners, lighthouse keepers and sailors all keeping the day. The spirit quotes Scrooge's own words about the surplus population back at him, and then lifts his robe on two starved children.

scenes.summary: A small goose made to go round, and Tiny Tim's blessing, immediately shadowed by the spirit's answer about the empty seat.
Scrooge watches himself become a parlour game and laughs before he can stop himself.
Two children under the robe, named as Man's and not the spirit's, with a warning about which of them is the more dangerous.

structure.label: Stave IV
structure.title: The Last of the Spirits
structure.summary: The final spirit says nothing at all, so Scrooge has to do the interpreting himself: businessmen bargaining over whether to attend a cheap funeral, a laundress selling bed-curtains stripped from a corpse, an unwatched body, and a family relieved by a death. Only at the grave is the name supplied.

scenes.summary: Merchants treat a death as a minor scheduling question, and Scrooge listens without recognising the subject.
The dead man's curtains, shirt and blankets are haggled over by the people who were nearest him at the end.
Scrooge asks whether these are shadows of what will be or only what may be, and reads his own name.

structure.label: Stave V
structure.title: The End of It
structure.summary: The bed-curtains are still hanging, which is the proof Scrooge wants. The last stave is deliberately made of errands — a turkey bought, a donation whispered, a dinner attended, a salary raised — because Dickens will not let the change stand as a private feeling.

scenes.summary: Scrooge laughs, sends the prize turkey to Camden Town anonymously, and pays for the cab.
He finds the charity collector of the day before and names a sum the text never discloses to the reader.
Bob Cratchit arrives eighteen and a half minutes late, is threatened with a raise, and is told to buy more coal.

characters.name: Ebenezer Scrooge
characters.role: Moneylender, surviving partner of Scrooge and Marley
characters.summary: A man whose coldness is described as a climate he carries about with him rather than a mood he is in. Dickens gives him wit, arguing with his own hallucination about undigested beef, which is why his conversion can be believed: the intelligence was never missing, only the use he put it to.
characters.clue: He argues that a ghost may be a crumb of cheese, reads his own name on a headstone, and ends by buying a turkey too big for a boy to carry.

characters.name: Jacob Marley
characters.summary: Seven years dead and still doing the accounts. He is punished not for cruelty but for a narrow definition of business, and his chain is made of the objects of his trade, which makes the moral visible before it is stated.
characters.clue: He wears cash-boxes, ledgers and keys as a chain, and corrects the meaning of one word in a way that sets up the whole book.

characters.name: Bob Cratchit
characters.summary: Fifteen shillings a week, a white comforter instead of a greatcoat, and a coal-box he is not allowed to reach. Dickens is careful to show him sliding on the ice at Cornhill on the way home, so that his goodness is not simply the patience of a man too tired to object.
characters.clue: He tries to warm himself at a candle, drinks a toast to the man who underpays him, and slides down a lane of boys on his way back to Camden Town.

characters.name: Tiny Tim
characters.summary: He has very few lines and one of them has escaped the book entirely. Dickens keeps him from being merely pathetic by giving him a thought of his own about being seen in church, which turns his visible disability into something he has decided how to use.
characters.clue: He is carried on his father's shoulder, hopes the congregation notices his crutch for a reason of his own, and speaks the last four words of the book.

characters.name: Fred
characters.summary: He makes the case for Christmas in one long unbroken sentence and admits within it that the season has never earned him a penny, which is the strongest argument available. He keeps inviting his uncle to dinner every year and is refused every year, and goes on asking.
characters.clue: He comes in glowing from the frost, argues that a season which has never made him any money has still done him good, and never stops inviting his uncle to dinner.

characters.name: Belle
characters.role: The woman Scrooge was engaged to
characters.summary: She releases him in the gentlest possible terms and the terms are devastating: their contract was made when they were both poor, he is a different man, and she asks whether he would choose her today. She is right, and he cannot answer.
characters.clue: She hands back an engagement without raising her voice, naming the golden idol that has taken her place.

characters.name: Mr Fezziwig
characters.role: The master Scrooge was apprenticed to
characters.summary: An employer who spends a few pounds on a party and buys an amount of happiness that Scrooge, watching, can only describe as a fortune. He is in the book to prove that the alternative to Scrooge's conduct exists inside commerce rather than outside it.
characters.clue: He calls a halt to work, has the shutters up in a minute, and turns a warehouse into a ballroom at very small expense.

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Past
characters.role: The first of the three spirits
characters.summary: A figure that is old and young at once, with a jet of light from its head that Scrooge keeps trying to cover. It offers no interpretation of anything it shows, which is the method: the scenes are left to do their own arguing.
characters.clue: Its light can be put out with a cap, and it answers every protest by showing one more thing.

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Present
characters.role: The second of the three spirits
characters.summary: A giant among heaped food who greets Scrooge as a man to be known better, and then spends the stave withholding comfort. He gives Scrooge's own words about the surplus population back to him unaltered, and finishes by opening his robe on two children he insists belong to mankind.
characters.clue: He sits on a throne of turkeys, geese and chestnuts, ages visibly in a single night, and keeps two starved children under his skirts.

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
characters.role: The third and last of the spirits
characters.summary: A shrouded shape that never speaks and only points. Because it supplies no commentary, every conclusion in the stave has to be reached by Scrooge himself, which is why the stave frightens him more than the chained ghost did.
characters.clue: It is draped, silent, and does nothing throughout but extend one hand.

themes.name: Whether a person can change
themes.summary: The book stakes everything on a claim most Victorian fiction makes slowly: that a settled character can be remade in one night. Dickens protects the claim by making the evidence cumulative rather than sudden, and by ending with actions rather than resolutions.
themes.development: Scrooge argues with the first ghost, watches the second in silence, and by the fourth is on the ground asking whether what he has seen is fixed. The last stave answers in errands.

themes.name: Poverty and responsibility
themes.summary: Dickens attacks a habit of thought rather than wealth as such. Scrooge's objection to charity is not that money is dear but that institutions already exist, and the book's method is to take him to the places where the institutional answer stops being available.
themes.development: The collectors are refused in Stave I; the same language is turned round on Scrooge in Stave III; Ignorance and Want make the argument visible before Stave IV shows what the refusal costs.

themes.name: Memory and time
themes.summary: The three spirits are three tenses, and the book's structure is a grammar lesson. What the past supplies is not nostalgia but evidence: Scrooge weeps at the schoolboy because he has been given the one perspective he has been refusing, his own.
themes.development: Past explains, present indicts, future threatens; Stave V collapses all three into a single morning in which Scrooge says he will live in all of them at once.

themes.name: Business and the meaning of a word
themes.summary: Marley's correction of one noun is the hinge of the whole book. Scrooge and Marley have treated business as a trade; the ghost redefines it as everything a person is answerable for, and the rest of the story tests the new definition against a turkey, a coal-box and a salary.
themes.development: Stated as doctrine by Marley, dramatised by Fezziwig as something an employer may actually do, and settled in Stave V when Scrooge raises a wage.

themes.name: Christmas and community
themes.summary: Christmas in the book is not a feeling but a set of doors: dinners, parties, toasts, games, the ship's crew and the lighthouse keepers. Its power over Scrooge is that it is happening whether or not he attends, and the spirits' argument is largely just to show him the attendance.
themes.development: Fred's speech puts the case; Stave III proves it across an absurd range of places; Stave IV shows the alternative, a death nobody feels obliged to attend.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: Scrooge's loneliness is presented as an achievement rather than an accident — something he has taken trouble over, warning human sympathy to keep its distance. The book's cruellest stroke is that the future it shows him is not damnation but simply more of the same, uninterrupted.
themes.development: The solitary oyster of Stave I becomes the solitary child of Stave II and the unattended body of Stave IV; the pattern is one life shown three times.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator who speaks openly to the reader, arguing, joking and insisting.
techniques.inThisBook: The book opens by haggling with the reader about a simile — what exactly is dead about a doornail — and only then explains that the point must be conceded or nothing wonderful can follow.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: An explicit comparison using like or as.
techniques.inThisBook: Scrooge is hard as flint, solitary as an oyster and dead as a doornail by proxy; in the last stave the same device returns inverted, as a feather, an angel, a schoolboy and a drunken man in one breath.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: Abstractions given bodies and names so an argument can be seen.
techniques.inThisBook: Ignorance and Want are children with names on them, and Marley's chain is a balance sheet made wearable; the technique lets Dickens put a social argument on stage without stopping the story.

techniques.name: Gothic machinery
techniques.definition: Bells, darkness, apparitions, graves and locked rooms used to produce dread.
techniques.inThisBook: Every Gothic device here is made to do moral work: the knocker, the clanking chain and the shrouded figure all produce evidence rather than atmosphere alone.

techniques.name: Structural repetition
techniques.definition: The same shape repeated with variations so that changes register.
techniques.inThisBook: Three spirits, three visitations, three refusals in Stave I answered by three acts of generosity in Stave V; the book is built so the reader can hear the rhyme.

techniques.name: Cold as character
techniques.definition: Weather and temperature used as a description of a person rather than a setting.
techniques.inThisBook: Scrooge carries his own low temperature about with him, ices his office in the dog-days and cannot be chilled by any wind — the metaphor is established before a single ghost appears.

quotations.text: Marley was dead, to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that.
quotations.context: The opening sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'to begin with' is doing two jobs: it dates the death and it flags the fact as a premise the reader has to accept before anything else can be built on it. Dickens spends the next paragraph arguing about doornails precisely so that the death itself slips past unexamined.

quotations.text: Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.
quotations.context: The first full description of Scrooge, before any action.
quotations.analysis: Three of the four terms are about being closed rather than being cruel, and the flint image concedes that the fire is in there and simply has never been struck. An oyster is also something that can be opened, which is a quiet promise the book will keep in eighty pages.

quotations.text: He carried his own low temperature always about with him; he iced his office in the dog-days, and didn’t thaw it one degree at Christmas.
quotations.context: Continuing the opening portrait of Scrooge.
quotations.analysis: The cold is not something he suffers but something he emits, which makes his effect on the people round him a physical fact rather than an opinion about his manners. 'One degree' turns the sentence into a measurement, the language Scrooge himself would use.

quotations.text: a good time; a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time; the only time I know of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely
quotations.speaker: Fred
quotations.context: Fred answering his uncle's demand to know what reason he has to be merry.
quotations.analysis: Fred's whole defence arrives as a single unbroken sentence with the clauses piling up, which is the opposite of Scrooge's clipped questions and refusals. He then concedes the accounting point — Christmas has never put gold or silver in his pocket — and argues that it has done him good anyway, meeting his uncle on his own ground and declining to stay there.

quotations.text: “Are there no prisons?” asked Scrooge.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: His first reply to the two gentlemen collecting for the poor.
quotations.analysis: He answers a request for money with a question about institutions, which moves the conversation from particular people to public provision and lets him leave without giving anything. Four words also make him sound reasonable, and the book has to spend three staves undoing that impression.

quotations.text: “If they would rather die,” said Scrooge, “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Told that many would rather die than go to the workhouse.
quotations.analysis: The phrase belongs to political economy rather than to malice: it treats people as a quantity in excess of a total. Dickens stores it carefully, and in Stave III has the Ghost of Christmas Present quote it back word for word while Scrooge is looking at a child who may be the one it applies to.

quotations.text: There’s more of gravy than of grave about you, whatever you are!
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Explaining to Marley's ghost why he will not believe in it.
quotations.analysis: A pun under that much pressure is a sign of nerve, and it tells us the man is not stupid, only committed. Dickens needs this joke: a Scrooge with no wit could be frightened into reform, and reform by fright alone is exactly what the last stave has to disprove.

quotations.text: “I wear the chain I forged in life,” replied the Ghost. “I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: Answering Scrooge's question about why he is fettered.
quotations.analysis: Free will is named twice in one sentence, which removes any suggestion that this is a punishment imposed from outside. The chain is made of cash-boxes, ledgers and keys, so what he is wearing is not a penalty for his trade but his trade itself, simply weighed.

quotations.text: “Business!” cried the Ghost, wringing its hands again. “Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence were, all, my business.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: After Scrooge says that Marley was always a good man of business.
quotations.analysis: The argument is won by repeating a single word until its meaning shifts under it: five uses of 'business' in three sentences, each one widening the term. Marley does not tell Scrooge to stop being a man of business; he tells him he has been doing a small part of the job and calling it the whole.

quotations.text: “It is required of every man,” the Ghost returned, “that the spirit within him should walk abroad among his fellow-men, and travel far and wide; and, if that spirit goes not forth in life, it is condemned to do so after death.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: Explaining what kind of afterlife he is serving.
quotations.analysis: The punishment is exactly the neglected duty, performed compulsorily and too late — the ghost is not in torment for anything he did but for a journey he declined to make. It also quietly explains the plot: Scrooge is about to be walked round London against his will.

quotations.text: “The school is not quite deserted,” said the Ghost. “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Past
quotations.context: Arriving at the schoolroom of Scrooge's boyhood.
quotations.analysis: The ghost describes the boy in the present tense and in the third person, so that Scrooge hears his own childhood reported as a piece of news about a stranger. 'Solitary' has already been used of the adult oyster, and the repetition makes the loneliness a continuous condition rather than a result.

quotations.text: He has the power to render us happy or unhappy; to make our service light or burdensome; a pleasure or a toil.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Defending Fezziwig after the spirit remarks that the ball cost only a few pounds.
quotations.analysis: Dickens notes that Scrooge says this 'speaking unconsciously like his former, not his latter self' — the argument for decent employment comes out of Scrooge's own mouth before he has agreed to it. It also states the case in the vocabulary of power and service, not charity, which is why it will hold in the final stave.

quotations.text: “It matters little,” she said softly. “To you, very little. Another idol has displaced me; and, if it can cheer and comfort you in time to come as I would have tried to do, I have no just cause to grieve.”
quotations.speaker: Belle
quotations.context: Releasing the young Scrooge from their engagement.
quotations.analysis: She accuses him of idolatry and then immediately withdraws her own standing to complain about it, which leaves him nothing to push against. 'Idol' is the strongest word in the sentence and the only religious one in a scene otherwise conducted entirely in the language of contracts.

quotations.text: “Come in!” exclaimed the Ghost. “Come in! and know me better, man!”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: Scrooge's first sight of the second spirit, among heaped food.
quotations.analysis: An invitation, not a summons — the opposite of Stave I, where Scrooge spent the whole evening refusing to come in or let anyone else. The word 'man' at the end is a greeting between equals, and it is the first time anyone in the book has addressed him with that kind of warmth.

quotations.text: He told me, coming home, that he hoped the people saw him in the church, because he was a cripple, and it might be pleasant to them to remember upon Christmas Day who made lame beggars walk and blind men see.
quotations.speaker: Bob Cratchit
quotations.context: Bob reporting what Tiny Tim said on the way back from church.
quotations.analysis: Tim has thought about how he is looked at and decided what he wants the looking to do, which makes him an agent in the scene rather than an object of pity. The thought reaches the reader at two removes — the child told his father, the father tells his wife — so the boy's dignity is never staged for effect.

quotations.text: “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all.
quotations.speaker: Tiny Tim
quotations.context: The end of the Cratchits' Christmas toast.
quotations.analysis: 'The last of all' places him at the end of a queue of speakers, the smallest voice in the room, and Dickens gives the line no emphasis whatever. It returns as the last sentence of the book, by which time the reader has been shown a future in which it was not said.

quotations.text: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want. Beware of them both, and all of their degree, but most of all beware this boy, for on his brow I see that written which is Doom, unless the writing be erased.
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: Revealing the two children clinging beneath his robe.
quotations.analysis: The spirit has just said the children are Man's, not his, which places the responsibility before the allegory arrives. Ignorance is ranked above Want as the greater danger, which is a specific political claim about schooling rather than relief, and 'unless the writing be erased' leaves the sentence open in a book whose whole subject is whether a foreseen end can still be changed.

quotations.text: “Are there no prisons?” said the Spirit, turning on him for the last time with his own words. “Are there no workhouses?”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: The spirit's final words, immediately after showing Ignorance and Want.
quotations.analysis: Nothing is added and nothing is explained; the whole rebuke consists of Scrooge's own sentences handed back at the right moment. Dickens has waited two staves to use them, and the delay is what gives the repetition its force — the reader recognises the words before Scrooge does.

quotations.text: Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of the things that May be only?
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: At the neglected grave, before he is made to read the name on it.
quotations.analysis: The question the whole book turns on, and the silent spirit refuses to answer it. Scrooge is asking about grammar — the difference between a future tense and a conditional — and the novella's position is that the difference is entirely made of what he does on Christmas morning.

quotations.text: I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Clutching at the robe of the last spirit, beside his own headstone.
quotations.analysis: He promises to keep all three tenses running at once, which is a precise description of what the book has just done to him. 'Try' is the honest word in the sentence: the vow is made in terror at a graveside, and Dickens leaves a whole stave to test whether it survives daylight.

quotations.text: I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy, I am as giddy as a drunken man.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Christmas morning, tangled in his own stockings.
quotations.analysis: The same device that fixed him in Stave I — hard as flint, solitary as an oyster — comes back running in the other direction, four similes where there had been four. Two of them, the schoolboy and the drunken man, restore exactly the parts of a life the earlier staves showed him losing.

quotations.text: Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did not die, he was a second father.
quotations.context: The narrator's account of what followed.
quotations.analysis: 'Who did not die' is slipped in as a subordinate clause, as though it were incidental, and it is the single most important fact in the book. Dickens measures the conversion by other people's outcomes rather than by Scrooge's feelings, which is why the sentence is about what he was to somebody rather than what he became.

quotations.text: And so, as Tiny Tim observed, “God Bless Us, Every One!”
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: The book closes by handing its last words to its smallest character, and by putting them in the past tense of reported speech — 'observed' — as though the blessing were a settled matter of record. The capitals are new since Stave III: the same four words, now printed as a title.

timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: The family's later collapse into debt gave him the clerk's-eye view of London money that runs through the novella.

timeline.label: Poor Law Amendment Act
timeline.detail: The workhouse system Scrooge names so confidently when he is asked for a donation.

timeline.label: Dickens speaks in Manchester
timeline.detail: He addressed the Athenaeum there in October, on education and poverty, weeks before beginning the book.

timeline.label: A Christmas Carol published
timeline.detail: Chapman and Hall issued it on 19 December as a gift book with gilt edges and John Leech's illustrations; the production costs cut deeply into Dickens's profit.

timeline.label: Stage versions within weeks
timeline.detail: Edward Stirling's adaptation opened at the Adelphi Theatre in February, one of several unauthorised dramatisations.

timeline.label: The Chimes
timeline.detail: Dickens follows the Carol with the second of five Christmas books, angrier and more directly political.

timeline.label: Dickens begins reading the Carol in public
timeline.detail: The first readings were given in Birmingham at the end of the year, and he went on performing an abridged text for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Dickens dies at Gad's Hill
timeline.detail: By then the public readings had made Scrooge a role as much as a character.

timeline.label: Scrooge; or, Marley's Ghost
timeline.detail: R. W. Paul's short film, among the earliest screen versions of any Dickens work.

timeline.label: Alastair Sim's Scrooge
timeline.detail: Brian Desmond Hurst's British film became one of the standard screen reference points for the part.

timeline.label: The Muppet Christmas Carol
timeline.detail: Brian Henson's film with Michael Caine keeps much of Dickens's narration by putting Gonzo on screen as the author.

places.name: City of London
places.note: Scrooge's counting house and the Exchange, where Stave IV opens among merchants discussing a funeral.

places.name: Cornhill
places.note: Bob Cratchit slides down the ice here twenty times on his way home on Christmas Eve.

places.name: Camden Town
places.note: The Cratchits' house, and the address the prize turkey has to be sent to by cab.

places.name: Manchester
places.note: Dickens spoke at the Athenaeum here in October 1843, shortly before writing the book.

criticalViews.position: A social argument in the shape of a fable
criticalViews.summary: Read alongside Dickens's public speaking of 1843 and the reports on child labour he had been reading, the book looks like an intervention in the poor-relief debate that chose allegory because allegory sells at Christmas.
criticalViews.counter: It leaves the remedy with individual generosity: Scrooge raises one salary, and nothing in the system he defended in Stave I has been touched.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading treats the book as a religious structure in secular dress — warning, examination of conscience, terror, penitence and works — with the spirits functioning as three stages of self-examination.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away how much of the change is produced by fear of a grave rather than by the memory and pity of the earlier staves.

criticalViews.summary: A long-running argument in cultural history holds that the novella did not invent the festival but fixed a particular version of it — domestic, charitable, sentimental — at the moment when Christmas print and gift-giving were expanding fastest.
criticalViews.counter: The claim is easy to overstate: carols, feasting and seasonal charity long predate 1843, and the book's popularity may record a change as much as cause it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens present Scrooge's transformation?
plan: Start with the Stave I portrait and note that the flint image already concedes the fire is present and unstruck.
Show the ghosts working by different methods: the past supplies evidence, the present indicts, the future threatens and says nothing.
Use the moment in Stave II where Scrooge defends Fezziwig 'unconsciously like his former, not his latter self' as the first sign of movement.
Argue about the mechanism: is he reformed by pity at the schoolroom, or by terror at the grave, and does the book need both?
Close on Stave V, where Dickens measures the change in turkeys, cab fares, coal and a salary rather than in feelings.

essayQuestions.question: What does A Christmas Carol say about poverty and responsibility?
essayQuestions.focus: The Poor Law, charity and the limits of the fable
plan: Open with the charity collectors: Scrooge answers a request for money with a question about institutions.
Track the phrase about the surplus population from Stave I to the moment the Ghost of Christmas Present returns it in Stave III.
Read Ignorance and Want closely, noting that the spirit calls them Man's and ranks Ignorance as the greater danger.
Set the Cratchit scenes against the Stave IV visit to old Joe's shop, where poverty produces theft rather than loyalty.
Weigh the ending: one employer improves, which may be the book's answer or the limit of it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens use the supernatural in the novella?
plan: Establish the ground rules: the narrator insists on Marley's death so that the return can mean something.
Compare the three spirits as three kinds of evidence — shown, opened and withheld.
Examine why the silent spirit frightens Scrooge most, and what work the silence forces him to do.
Look at Marley's chain as an allegory that is also a stage property, visible to an audience at a public reading.
Decide whether the supernatural machinery makes the social argument sharper or lets the reader off it.

essayQuestions.question: 'The book's real subject is time, not money.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Past, present and future as structure
plan: Set out the design: three spirits, three tenses, and a story that takes one night to cover a lifetime.
Use the schoolroom and Belle's release to show the past functioning as evidence rather than nostalgia.
Note how Stave III insists on simultaneity — miners, sailors and a lighthouse all keeping the day at once.
Test the case on Scrooge's question at the grave about shadows of what will be and what may be only.
Answer with Stave IV's vow to live in all three tenses at once, and ask whether money or time is what he has been wasting.

discussionQuestions: The last spirit never speaks. Does that make it more frightening than Marley, and if so why?
Scrooge raises one clerk's wages. Is that a solution to anything the book has described?
Dickens calls the divisions staves and the book a carol. What does the musical framing change about how you read it?
Tiny Tim has very few lines. Is he a character or a device, and does the distinction matter?
Would the conversion be as convincing if Stave V ended in the bedroom rather than in the street?

related.why: The Christmas book Dickens wrote next, with the same machinery turned to a much angrier argument about the deserving poor.
The last of the Christmas books, and the inverse experiment: a man granted the power to forget.
Dickens twenty years later on the same question of what money does to a person's judgement of the people who raised them.
The domestic side of the Christmas books, and a useful contrast with the Carol's social sharpness.
The customs, food and print culture the novella arrived in and helped to shape.
